📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, today, we’re announcing AWS Lambda Web Functions, a new form factor that lets you run standard HTTP web applications on Lambda without rewriting your code into an event handler. You can take a standard port-listening server built with Express, Hono, Fastify, Next.js, or any Node.js framework, deploy it with a single command, and Lambda automatically handles scaling, multi-region distribution, and active CPU billing. No adapters, no infrastructure to manage, and no framework lock-in.

With this launch, AWS Lambda now offers three distinct form factors, each built on the same Firecracker isolation technology and designed for a different programming model.

In a recent development, lambda Event Functions are what you already know as Lambda functions. They use the event-driven, single-concurrent handler model with wall-clock billing. We’re introducing the “Event Functions” name to highlight that programming model: your function receives an event, processes it, and returns a response. The event-driven programming model is ideal for event processing, queue consumers, and invocations triggered by other AWS services.

Recent findings suggest that lambda Web Functions use an HTTP-native programming model with multi-concurrent execution and active CPU billing. Your code listens on a port and handles standard HTTP requests. That programming model is ideal for web applications, API backends, and interactive HTTP workloads where multiple concurrent requests and I/O-heavy processing are the norm.

Lambda MicroVMs provide isolated, stateful sandbox environments with customer-managed lifecycles for running untrusted or user-generated code.

It has been revealed that the three complement each other. An application might use Event Functions for asynchronous backend processing, Web Functions for the user-facing API and server-side rendering layer, and MicroVMs for interactive code execution features, all within the same AWS account and sharing the same operational model.

Why Web FunctionsModern web applications need to serve global audiences with fast, consistent response times while giving developers the freedom to use standard frameworks and iterate swiftly. Building this today typically requires assembling multiple infrastructure components, configuring multi-region deployments, setting up latency-based routing, and tuning billing models to avoid paying for I/O wait. Developers often find themselves adapting their application code to fit a specific compute model rather than deploying the HTTP server they already have.

Lambda Web Functions removes this complexity. Each execution environment handles multiple requests simultaneously (up to 128 concurrent requests per environment), which means a burst of incoming traffic can share warm environments instead of mapping each request to a new one. Web Functions meter the CPU time your code uses, so time spent waiting on a database query or an API call consumes little CPU. Memory is metered for as long as the execution environment exists. For I/O-heavy web workloads like server-side rendering, API backends, and AI inference endpoints streaming token responses, this can reduce compute costs.

Sources indicate that let’s try it outTo get started, I wrote a simple Express.js server. This is the same code I run locally with node index.js, no Lambda-specific adapters or wrappers required.

It has been revealed that the only difference from running locally is the AWS_LAMBDA_HTTP_ENDPOINT environment variable, which Lambda sets to the host and port your server must listen on. To run locally, set it yourself, for example AWS_LAMBDA_HTTP_ENDPOINT=127.0.0.1:3000 node index.js.

With my code ready, I deployed using the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI):.

In a recent development, one command. No prior resource setup. The CLI bundled my source, created the Web Function, published its first revision, attached a Web Function endpoint, and returned a live HTTPS URL in under a minute.

A revision is an immutable snapshot of the code I deployed. The endpoint is the HTTPS URL that routes traffic to a revision, or splits traffic across revisions. Those are the resources I use to iterate and to control how traffic moves to fresh code.

Recent findings suggest that next, I wanted my application to serve users in Europe and Asia with lower latency. I redeployed with multiple regions:.

In a recent development, lambda Web Functions replicated my code to all three regions and configured latency-based routing automatically. Each request now routes to the Region with the lowest latency for the caller, on a best-effort basis, through one global URL (.lambda-web.global.on.aws).

According to recent reports, when I updated my code and ran the same deploy command again, the CLI detected the existing function, uploaded the upcoming revision, and pointed the endpoint at it. Total turnaround from code change to live: seconds.

For production workflows that require a more gradual rollout, I can shift traffic between revisions with a single API call:.

This sends 90% of endpoint traffic to the current revision and 10% to the new one, giving me a canary deployment without additional tooling.

It has been revealed that better together with Amazon CloudFrontFor applications that combine static and dynamic content, Web Functions works well alongside Amazon CloudFront. You can select a Web Function endpoint as the origin for your CloudFront distribution. Static assets are served from the cache while dynamic requests route to your Web Function, giving you CDN performance for static content with serverless compute for the dynamic parts.

Web Functions improves the private-origin experience with CloudFront. With this launch, you attach CloudFront origin access control (OAC) to a Web Function endpoint instead. CloudFront signs requests to the origin, and the endpoint allows only your distribution to invoke it. You get the same private-origin pattern CloudFront already provides for Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), without exposing the endpoint or adding custom authorization to your app.

Industry observers note that now availableAWS Lambda Web Functions is available today in US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), and Europe (Ireland). Web Functions run Node.js 24 (nodejs24.x) on Arm64 at launch and support Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) connectivity, allowing your function to access resources that exist within a VPC.

To get started, deploy your first Web Function in under a minute:.

For pricing details, visit the AWS Lambda pricing page. To learn more, see the Lambda Web Functions documentation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some numbers are hard to picture until you sit with them for a moment. Last week we published the Prime Day 2026 metrics, and the one that stuck with me is 2.3 quadrillion: the daily requests Amazon ElastiCache peaked at during the event. Prime Day ran back in June, so this post always lands as a retrospective, and that gap is part of what makes it worth reading. By the time the numbers reach you, the only evidence that any of it happened is that nothing went wrong.

The rest of the week pulled in a different direction: smaller, cheaper, and more constrained. Claude Haiku 5.5 arrived on Amazon Bedrock at roughly 75 percent less than Haiku 4.5, Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic made voice agents quicker on their feet, and Strands Box showed up to put real boundaries around what an agent is allowed to do. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news….

According to recent reports, headlinesAll the numbers: Amazon Prime Day 2026 powered by AWS is the latest entry in a tradition that goes back to 2016, and the scale is still difficult to hold in your head. Over the four days of Prime Day, Amazon DynamoDB processed more than 59 trillion requests while peaking at 192 million requests per second, and kept single-digit millisecond responses throughout. AWS Lambda handled over 2.3 trillion invocations per day. Amazon EBS peaked above 24.8 trillion I/O operations, moving more than an exabyte of data daily. Amazon ECS rolled out an average of 158.3 million tasks per day on AWS Fargate, a 47.7 percent jump over last year, and AWS Graviton powered up to 49 percent of the Amazon EC2 compute that Amazon.com used.

Sources indicate that the number I keep coming back to, though, isn’t a throughput record. The team ran more than 44,000 AWS Fault Injection Service experiments ahead of the event, more than six times what they ran in 2025. Those are deliberate failures injected on purpose, months in advance, so that the trillions of requests above turn into an ordinary shopping afternoon. If you’re preparing for your own peak moment, AWS Countdown Premium is built for exactly that kind of planning.

Tech Report: AI found more critical bugs in another widely used technology running 225M websites

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (792 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theregister

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hot on the heels of serious vulnerabilities in seemingly every other widely used software powering the entire internet, F5 today released emergency patches for 10 bugs in open source NGINX.
  • These include critical remote code execution flaws that let attackers hijack NGINX servers with HTTP/2 enabled, as well as the millions of websites running NGINX, to steal sensitive data and disrupt services.
  • Recent findings suggest that “At this time, we have found no evidence of active exploitation of any of these vulnerabilities in the wild,” and F5 spokesperson told The Register.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Open source NGINX joins patchapalooza.

Hot on the heels of serious vulnerabilities in seemingly every other widely used software powering the entire internet, F5 today released emergency patches for 10 bugs in open source NGINX.

These include critical remote code execution flaws that let attackers hijack NGINX servers with HTTP/2 enabled, as well as the millions of websites running NGINX, to steal sensitive data and disrupt services.

Recent findings suggest that “At this time, we have found no evidence of active exploitation of any of these vulnerabilities in the wild,” and F5 spokesperson told The Register. “We continue to monitor closely and will share updates via myF5 as we learn more.”.

It has been revealed that as with all of the other recently disclosed vulnerabilities in foundational technologies like PHP, Apache, and Java, these critical NGINX bugs were uncovered by researchers using AI. One of them has been hiding in the code for at least 10 years.

Tomer Schwartz, Wiz’s chief technology officer of exposure management and AppSec, helped find the bug, along with researchers from Ikotas Labs, Metnir, Rapid7, and Xint working independently.

Schwartz told The Register that this wave of AI-discovered flaws “point to a newly introduced reality.”.

Industry observers note that “We need to treat every internet-connected system as potentially vulnerable,” Schwartz said. “AI has changed not only which vulnerabilities can be found, but how swiftly longstanding risks can become real threats.”.

According to recent reports, NGINX is the world’s most widely used open source web server, handling HTTPS requests and routing incoming traffic to the right application or API. It powers about a third of all websites (around 225 million), and F5 maintains the open source version.

On Wednesday, F5 published an out-of-band security notification that addressed 10 CVEs in open source NGINIX. If you run NGINX, update to 1.31.9 as soon as possible.

Two of the vulns are especially serious as they allow a remote attacker to execute code on the NGINX server without authentication. These two, tracked as CVE-2026-123633 and CVE-2026-123007, both received a critical, 9.2 CVSS rating, and CVE-2026-123007 affects versions dating back to NGINX 1.9.5 in 2015. Both vulnerabilities require HTTP/2 to be enabled on the affected NGINX server.

All of the security shops listed earlier independently found at least one of these two CVEs - most, if not all, with an AI assist - and reported them to F5.

“Both vulnerabilities are memory-safety complications in how NGINX handles HTTP/2 traffic,” Schwartz and fellow Wiz kid Nir Ohfeld remarked in a Wednesday blog about the two bugs. “In CVE-2026-123633, a connection's memory is freed while a request still needs it, creating a use-after-free. In CVE-2026-123007, incorrect flow-control accounting leads to an invalid memory copy.”.

Rapid7’s team also published a proof-of-concept to demonstrate leveraging CVE-2026-123007 for unauthenticated remote code execution against a vulnerable linux/amd64 Docker image running nginx version 1.31.8.

Xint found three other NGINX flaws, plus a separate vulnerability in the Linux kernel that can be chained with any of the five NGINX vulnerabilities to gain root privileges on the host. The research team dubbed the six bugs “nginx2root.”.

Industry observers note that the AI-powered offensive security firm also published videos demonstrating attacks using CVE-2026-123007 to execute commands as the NGINX worker inside a container, and then using the kernel vulnerability to escalate to root on the host. These attacks work on AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud Platform, and bare-metal servers.

According to recent reports, "While preparing for ZeroDay Cloud 2026, a Xint researcher found CVE-2026-123007," the company noted in a Wednesday blog. "A few days later, a fully automated Xint scan found the other four without human guidance.".

All of these newly-disclosed CVEs point to a larger security issue - especially in light of Tuesday’s Java4Shell, found by AI-bug-hunting-outfit Calif, PHP2Shell (Calif was one of the firms that also used AI to find and weaponize these critical vulns in PHP), and a critical Apache flaw under active exploitation .

“AI is also accelerating vulnerability discovery faster than existing infrastructure was designed to absorb,” Schwartz told us. “Even after a vendor ships a fix, security teams still face heavy manual work in terms of locating vulnerable versions and configurations, testing patches, deploying interim mitigations (such as disabling HTTP/2), and coordinating all of these rollouts.”.

There is light at the end of the tunnel, he believes. “In the long run, AI-powered vulnerability research will harden foundational software.”.

But in the meantime, it’s a nightmare for security teams, vulnerability managers, and system administrators, who are drowning in the near-daily deluge of CVEs to patch before attackers find and exploit these vulnerabilities.

“Continued collaboration between security researchers, maintainers, and defenders is crucial to absorb the speed and scale of these disclosures,” Schwartz mentioned.®.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, to celebrate, we are shipping with Meta day-0 support in transformers, llama.cpp, vLLM, Inference Endpoints, and other libraries.
  • Sources indicate that scores are reported as published.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Great news from the OGs of open source LLMs! Muse Glimmer, released today, is Meta’s upcoming multimodal model, especially designed for local agentic use cases. Distilled from Muse to 30B parameters, and released under the Apache 2.0 license, it’s ideal deploying locally for privacy, reducing costs, or just hacking around. It’s intended for privacy-aware applications such as coding, document analysis, personal assistants, Claw- or Hermes-like setups.

In a recent development, to celebrate, we are shipping with Meta day-0 support in transformers, llama.cpp, vLLM, Inference Endpoints, and other libraries. We built a few cool things and explain our findings in this blog.

Check out the demos below for inspiration.

You can find Muse Glimmer on the Hugging Face Hub.

Sources indicate that scores are reported as published. Bold indicates the best result among the compared models; ↓ indicates lower is better.

Muse Glimmer is a dense 30B parameter model consisting of:.

According to recent reports, in addition to the main VLM, there’s also a speculative decoding drafter implemented on DFlash. Usage of this module is optional, and it can provide much faster generation in exchange for some memory cost. We found this drafter to be particularly well suited to structured content generation such as coding.

The language model uses the following architecture components:.

Muse Glimmer uses one image encoder to handle both images and videos. Unlike the relatively small vision encoders used in other VLMs, this is a sizable 2B ViT-like model designed after the Perception Encoder architecture. Perception Encoder was previously introduced by Meta as a backbone for various downstream spatial and multimodal tasks.The encoder patchifies images to a shape of 2 frames x 3 channels x 14 x 14, and passes them through a linear layer for projection. An interpolated absolute position embedding from a learned position table is then added to these embeddings. These are then sent to the vision tower which consist of 50 layers and GELU MLPs. Similar to the language model, the attention pattern consists of three window attention layers followed by one full attention layer. Inside the attention layers, 2D RoPE is applied to the queries and keys.

After transformer, pixel shuffle concatenates 2x2 groups of neighboring spatial tokens which reduces the number of image tokens 4x without discarding their channels. The merged features are then projected to the shared embedding space of the text decoder.

Recent findings suggest that videos go through the same encoder frame by frame, where each frame is converted into patches (of shape [batch, temporal groups, grid height, grid width, 2 frames, 3 channels, 14, 14]). The processor targets 2 frames per second and caps the clip at 96 frames sampled evenly across video. The processor creates timestamped video placeholders, interleaving text with frame e.g. “Time: 0.0s <|video|> x N” in which the final video embeddings are replaced before the final projection layer.

Upgrade transformers to the latest version to be able to use Muse Glimmer.

Sources indicate that you can use TRL to fine-tune Muse Glimmer using various methods from SFT to Async GRPO. We have run two experiments on bf16 with Hopper-class GPUs with 80GB VRAM each.

Sources indicate that we also experimented with running the model on OpenCode with AsyncGRPO example. Model highlights strong coding capabilities, so we encourage you to try training with coding environments in OpenEnv and TRL.

Recent findings suggest that here are some fun ways to try out Muse Glimmer. In our opinion, the coolest thing about this model is that it is a local scale personal assistant that can code. That means you can make it do things like, quantize itself, find quantized weights on the Hub, deploy itself to inference endpoints, and even optimize itself for specific hardware! Let’s go team local 🚀.

Assume the Inference Endpoint exposes an OpenAI-compatible /v1 API.

It also connects to the official Hugging Face MCP server, giving the agent read-only tools to search and inspect Hub repositories, models, datasets, Spaces, documentation, and papers.

Industry observers note that we are happy to welcome Muse Glimmer to the Hugging Face Hub. Try Muse Glimmer with your local coding setups today!

Recent findings suggest that timing is a bit suspicious Meta faced about $1B in fines over child-safety failures specifically a Upcoming Mexico judge found its platforms were harming children and that Meta didn’t warn the public about the dangers. now it’s releasing a cheaper API so others pay the fines, damage control.

It has been revealed that muse Glimmer uses one image encoder to handle both images and videos. Unlike the relatively small vision encoders used in other VLMs, this is a sizable 2B ViT-like model designed after the Perception Encoder architecture. Perception Encoder was previously introduced by Meta as moviebox a backbone for various downstream spatial and multimodal tasks.The encoder patchifies images to a shape of 2 frames x 3 channels x 14 x 14, and passes them through a linear layer for projection. An interpolated absolute position embedding from a learned position table is then added to these embeddings. These are then sent to the vision tower which consist of 50 layers and GELU MLPs. Similar to the language model, the attention pattern consists of three window attention layers followed by one full attention layer. Inside the attention layers, 2D RoPE is applied to the queries and keys.

It has been revealed that after transformer, pixel shuffle concatenates 2x2 groups of neighboring spatial tokens which reduces the number of image tokens 4x without discarding their channels. The merged features are then projected to the shared embedding space of the text decoder.

According to recent reports, muse Glimmer looks like a really exciting step for practical open-source AI, especially with its focus on local, agentic, and multimodal workloads. A 30B-parameter model combining a 2B vision encoder with a 28B text decoder gives developers a strong foundation for coding, document analysis, personal assistants, and other privacy-sensitive applications. 🔥🤖.

It has been revealed that the Apache 2.0 license is another major highlight because it makes the model much more approachable for developers who want to experiment, customize, and deploy without relying entirely on hosted inference. Local deployment can also bring meaningful benefits around privacy, latency, and infrastructure costs, which makes this especially interesting for personal and enterprise workflows. 🚀.

I also like the architectural choices here, particularly the hybrid attention pattern, grouped-query attention, and Q-K normalization. Alternating sliding-window and full-attention layers seems like a thoughtful way to balance long-context capability with efficiency, while sharing KV heads across query heads can significantly reduce memory requirements during generation.

The day-zero ecosystem support makes the release even more compelling. Having integrations across Transformers, llama.cpp, vLLM, and other tools means developers can start testing real-world workflows immediately instead of waiting for the surrounding ecosystem to catch up. Open multimodal models that are genuinely practical to run locally could be a huge part of where AI development goes next. 💡👏.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, developers building web and AI applications on Vercel can now add Amazon S3 storage resources directly from the Vercel Marketplace and v0, combining the durability, scalability, and performance of S3 with the convenience of Vercel’s provisioning workflow. Starting today, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), including Amazon S3 Tables and Amazon S3 Vectors, is natively available on the Vercel Marketplace and v0 by Vercel, covering three distinct workloads: everyday storage, analytics, and AI.

In a recent development, why this matters Millions of developers build, deploy, and scale web and AI applications on Vercel. Storage is essential to performant applications, but provisioning it previously required navigating to the AWS Management Console to configure policies and credentials. Now, S3 storage integrates directly into the Vercel developer experience, with resource provisioning and connection configuration handled automatically. Together with existing integrations for Amazon Aurora, Amazon DynamoDB, and Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, you get a complete application stack inside Vercel (from your database layer through to object, vector, and open table storage), all on one AWS account with one bill.

Figure 1 – The AWS page on the Vercel Marketplace.

Getting started From the Vercel dashboard, go to the Storage tab and choose Create. Select AWS, pick your S3 bucket type, choose a Region, and create the bucket. Provisioning takes a few seconds.

Figure 2 – Creating an Amazon S3 general purpose bucket in Vercel by choosing a Region and a name.

Connect the bucket to a project, then pull the environment variables with the Vercel CLI:.

Sources indicate that the integration injects AWS_REGION, AWS_ROLE_ARN, AWS_RESOURCE_ARN, and a bucket name such as S3_BUCKET_NAME, S3_TABLE_BUCKET_NAME, or S3_VECTOR_BUCKET_NAME. At runtime, the awsCredentialsProvider from @vercel/functions/oidc exchanges a short-lived OIDC token with AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) for temporary credentials scoped to your resource. No static keys are stored anywhere.

Object storage with S3 This Next.js route uploads a file to a general purpose bucket:.

Use ListObjectsV2Command and GetObjectCommand with the same client to list and read objects.

Analytics with S3 Tables S3 Tables offer S3 storage purpose-built for analytics and are designed to automatically optimize query performance as data volumes grow. They provide fully managed Apache Iceberg tables with automated table maintenance and compaction, and they work with any Apache Iceberg REST Catalog-compliant engine. You can use DuckDB inside a Vercel Function for lightweight queries. This example attaches the table bucket by its ARN and runs an aggregate query:.

If you run DuckDB inside a Next.js route, add @duckdb/node-api to serverExternalPackages in next.config.mjs so the native bindings are not bundled.

Vector search with S3 Vectors S3 Vectors deliver purpose-built, cost-optimized vector storage for AI agents, AI inference, and semantic search of your content stored in Amazon S3. S3 Vectors provides native support for storing and querying vectors without a separate vector database, but it does not generate them. Create the embeddings with your model of choice, then query the index for the closest matches:.

Building with v0 by Vercel From v0, describe what you want to build and it provisions the right resource. Ask for “a photo gallery where customers upload images using AWS” to get a general purpose bucket, “a support bot that answers questions from my PDFs” to get S3 Vectors, or “an analytics dashboard for my clickstream data” to get S3 Tables. v0 then configures the connection and generates working code.

Figure 3 – v0 generating a PDF support bot from a natural language prompt, with Amazon S3 Vectors connected and the application in the Preview panel.

Combining S3 with AWS databases Every AWS service on Vercel shares the same account and authentication model, so you can combine them with no extra setup. For example, store file metadata in Aurora with the files in S3, or store document text in DynamoDB with embeddings in S3 Vectors for RAG retrieval.

Recent findings suggest that using Vercel with your AWS account You can create a fresh AWS account through the integration, which supports S3 features for building and testing. You can also link an existing AWS account to use your full set of S3 and AWS capabilities and keep your current billing. If you link an existing AWS account, Vercel works only with new buckets that you create through the platform. Because every S3 resource lives in your own AWS account, you keep AWS-native tooling and a single place to manage storage.

Pricing and availability There is no charge for the integration, and you pay standard Amazon S3 pricing for the resources you use. Upcoming AWS accounts created through Vercel receive $100 in credits valid for six months. Amazon S3, including S3 Tables and S3 Vectors, is available from v0 and the Vercel Marketplace in all commercial AWS Regions supported by Vercel. To get started, visit v0 or the AWS page on the Vercel Marketplace.

Making Knowledge Distillation Cheap Enough to Run at Scale

📅 10 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1199 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that knowledge distillation, training a smaller student model to match the performance of a larger teacher, is a well-known technique in Machine Learning.
  • In a recent development, the distillation step is what decides most of the final quality, but it's also usually the most expensive part of the pipeline.
  • It has been revealed that the standard setup, online distillation using the Kullback-Leibler divergence loss (KL loss), keeps both the teacher and the student loaded at the same time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that knowledge distillation, training a smaller student model to match the performance of a larger teacher, is a well-known technique in Machine Learning. With the recent wave of open-source Large Language Models, such as gpt-oss, Qwen, GLM, or Kimi, it has become a mainstream research topic again. Deploying these very large models is expensive: the recent Kimi-K3 model has 2.8 trillion parameters and needs roughly 3TB of VRAM just to load. Compressing them into smaller models and recovering the original capabilities through knowledge distillation has therefore become standard practice, with companies like Nvidia (Nemotron 3 Puzzle 75B) or Multiverse Computing (Hypernova 60B) recently releasing high-quality compressed models.

In a recent development, the distillation step is what decides most of the final quality, but it's also usually the most expensive part of the pipeline. Keeping both the teacher and student loaded, and producing a probability distribution over the entire vocabulary for every token, requires enormous amounts of VRAM, typically feasible only with hundreds of GPUs and careful tensor-parallelism strategies. Our latest paper, Efficient Knowledge Distillation for LLMs: Offline Top-K Logits and a Fused Chunked KL Loss, tackles this with two systems changes: caching the teacher's top-K logits once so the teacher never has to sit in memory alongside the student, and a new, memory-efficient KL-divergence loss that avoids ever materializing the full vocabulary-size × sequence-length matrix, cutting VRAM use far below what the default implementations in libraries like PyTorch or NVIDIA Megatron-Bridge achieve. Together, these two changes cut training cost enough to make long-context healing possible on a single GPU, and cheap enough to make large-scale experimentation practical.

It has been revealed that the standard setup, online distillation using the Kullback-Leibler divergence loss (KL loss), keeps both the teacher and the student loaded at the same time. At every training step, the teacher runs a full forward pass to produce its output distribution, and the student is trained to match it. This is the most expressive setup, since the full teacher distribution is available, but it is also the most memory- and compute-intensive: two full-vocabulary tensors have to be held per token position, and the teacher has to be recomputed on every single step even though its behavior does not change across a training run.

As a practical example, gpt-oss-120b has a vocabulary of 201,088 tokens. At a sequence length of 32K and batch size 4, the teacher-probability tensor alone has shape 4 × 201,088 × 32,768; in bfloat16, that's already about 50GB of VRAM for a single tensor. Add gradients, activations, model weights, and optimizer states, and a single training iteration of distillation can peak at roughly 250GB of VRAM, more than even an H200 or B200 GPU can provide. In this post, we show that reformulating the KL loss to process the data in chunks reduces this cost to almost nothing.

In a recent development, dense KL spikes to roughly 250GB, above a single H200's 141GB capacity. The fused chunked loss never forms that spike and peaks at about 128GB. Source: paper Figure 1.

Offline distillation. Instead of recomputing the teacher at every step, we compute its output once, cache the top-100 most likely tokens per position, and train the student against that cache. The teacher never has to sit in memory during training and does not need to be run again once the cache exists, so the same cache can be reused across many ablations.

It has been revealed that A fused, chunked KL loss. To see why the loss itself is expensive, picture what it actually builds: for every token position in a sequence and every word in the vocabulary, the loss needs a number describing how much the student's prediction disagrees with the teacher's. Laid out as a grid, that's one row per vocabulary entry and one column per sequence position, for a vocabulary of 100K+ words and a long sequence, that grid is enormous, and the default way of computing a KL loss builds the whole thing before it can produce a single number.

We compare three ways of computing this same loss, all mathematically equivalent:.

The GIF below reveals the difference between the dense and fused-chunked approaches: one builds the whole comparison grid and holds onto all of it, the other builds and discards one slice at a time, so memory never grows beyond a single chunk.

We have open-sourced the chunked-loss implementation: github.com/CompactifAI/Full-Chunked-KL-Loss.

In a recent development, the table below puts all four setups head to head: online distillation, and the three offline loss implementations just described. Comparing them on a single H200 GPU with Llama 3.1 8B Instruct as teacher and a 3.2B Llama model as student at an 8K token context, all four reach near-identical training loss, even though the offline runs train against only the cached top-100 logits per token.

The loss curves overlap almost exactly across all four methods, confirming offline distillation with top-100 cached logits is lossless relative to online distillation. Source: paper Figure 2. At this sequence length, the fused chunked loss is not yet the fastest option, its extra backward-pass projection costs a bit of speed, but its real advantage only indicates up as context length grows, which the next section demonstrates.

To see the scaling pattern more starkly, we ran an isolated benchmark on a toy output-projection network (no transformer body, just the loss kernel). At 32K tokens, peak memory falls from 85.2 GiB with the dense loss to 5.45 GiB with the fully chunked version, a 15.6× reduction, and the dense loss fails outright from 64K tokens onward. At 256K tokens, the fully chunked loss uses 11.6 GiB against 134.2 GiB for the next-best chunked variant, and is about 3.3× faster per iteration at that length.

Industry observers note that distilling a GPT-OSS 20B model at a 32,768-token context, the memory freed by the fused loss let the setup shrink from four GPU nodes down to one. Step time fell from 57.0 to 12.23 seconds, about 5× faster, and throughput per GPU rose from 74.2 to 345.7 TFLOP/s.

Sources indicate that the efficient offline setup is what made a large-scale distillation campaign affordable in the first place. The resulting compact student, distilled from Llama 3.1 8B Instruct down to about 3.2B parameters, retains most of the teacher's accuracy on BoolQ and HellaSwag, stays within about nine points of it on MMLU, at less than half the parameter count.

In a recent development, the student retains most of the teacher's short-context accuracy at less than half the size. Source: paper Figure 6.

This work is part of Multiverse Computing's ongoing research into making distillation and healing practical to run at scale, not just as a one-off recipe, but as something teams can iterate on cheaply. The paper also covers additional ablations, such as how the choice of loss function and sequence packing affect recovery quality.

Recent findings suggest that want the full technical details, including the closed-form gradient behind the fused chunked loss and the complete training configuration? Read the full paper, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying this to your own distillation pipelines.

We have also open-sourced the chunked-loss implementation: github.com/CompactifAI/Full-Chunked-KL-Loss.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that nothing last week added a latest kind of compute.
  • The counterweight arrived on Thursday.
  • In a recent development, headlinesAWS Lambda Web Functions is a newly introduced form factor that runs a standard HTTP web application on Lambda without rewriting it into an event handler.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that nothing last week added a latest kind of compute. What it did instead was shorten the distance between the code you already have and that code being live. AWS Lambda learned to run a plain HTTP server with no adapter in front of it, and Amazon S3 became something you can provision from inside the tool you were already using, without opening the AWS Management Console. Different services, same direction.

The counterweight arrived on Thursday. As it gets easier to put things into production, it matters more that you can say what those things are allowed to do, and this week’s most interesting read is about exactly that. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news….

In a recent development, headlinesAWS Lambda Web Functions is a newly introduced form factor that runs a standard HTTP web application on Lambda without rewriting it into an event handler. You take a port-listening server built with Express, Hono, Fastify, or Next.js, run aws lambda-web deploy, and get back a live HTTPS URL in under a minute. No adapters, no infrastructure to set up first, no framework lock-in. Lambda now has three form factors on the same Firecracker isolation, which compose inside one application: Event Functions (the model you already know) for async work, Web Functions for the user-facing layer, and MicroVMs for stateful sandboxes running untrusted code.

Two details make this more than repackaging. Each execution environment handles up to 128 concurrent requests, so a burst of traffic shares warm environments instead of mapping one request to one environment, and billing meters the CPU time your code actually uses rather than wall-clock time. For server-side rendering, API backends, and inference endpoints streaming tokens, where most of the elapsed time is spent waiting, that changes the arithmetic. Adding --regions to the same deploy command replicates your code and configures latency-based routing behind a single global URL, and you can split traffic across revisions by weight for a canary rollout. It’s available in five Regions, running Node.js 24 on Arm64 with VPC connectivity. The AWS Compute Blog has a longer walkthrough, and Amazon CloudFront can now use a Web Function endpoint as an origin with origin access control.

It has been revealed that the week’s other headline isn’t a launch. Trust in Depth: giving agents more autonomy without losing control makes an argument I keep running into in practice: putting a person in the loop for every agent action works at small scale and then quietly stops working, because people asked to check everything stop catching what matters. The alternative is four questions answered at four moments, which AWS calls scope, know, bound, and observe. The part worth sitting with is that an agent’s limits belong outside its own reasoning, in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore policies enforced at the gateway, because an agent cannot turn off a control it does not run. AWS has run automated reasoning in production for more than a decade, including AWS Identity and Access Management at more than 2.1 billion requests per second, and the case here is for pointing it at the rules you write for agents.

Another critical PHP security release has dropped

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (491 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Theregister

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • At least one dangerous RCE bug got a fix on Thursday.
  • It has been revealed that apologies in advance to all patch managers and security teams that thought they might get a break this week.
  • These fortunately were not leaked leaked like last month’s critical PHP2Shell flaws – but a Wednesday advisory warned, “The issues rated critical require either non-default configuration or uncommon setups,” urging PHP users to “prepare to upgrade promptly once the releases become available.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At least one dangerous RCE bug got a fix on Thursday.

It has been revealed that apologies in advance to all patch managers and security teams that thought they might get a break this week. The PHP Foundation has released several more patches, covering all supported versions, and including at least one rated “critical.”.

These fortunately were not leaked leaked like last month’s critical PHP2Shell flaws – but a Wednesday advisory warned, “The issues rated critical require either non-default configuration or uncommon setups,” urging PHP users to “prepare to upgrade promptly once the releases become available.”.

One of the vulnerabilities is another remote code execution (RCE) flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-115560.

In October, the PHP Foundation told The Register that it had reserved this CVE identifier for another RCE bug, but added it would not get an emergency fix like the earlier two PHP2Shell vulnerabilities because the third one doesn't pose the same risk.

Industry observers note that CVE-2026-115560 “requires a very unlikely combination of configuration and specific PHP application code, which we do not expect to occur in practical use of PHP,” Elizabeth Barron, executive director of the PHP Foundation, told The Register at the time. “The problem can be mitigated with a configuration setting. So for the moment the PHP Security Team has only published an informational advisory on the PHP website, explaining exactly this situation.”.

The earlier informational advisory urged people to “set session.upload_progress.enabled=0 until the next regular bugfix release, to fully protect from an unlikely RCE vector.”.

These unlikely RCE attacks require an application to set “session.serialize_handler to php_binary or php_serialize in its configuration and then switch it to php at runtime with ini_set() before calling session_start().”.

Additionally, the session upload progress feature must be enabled, which the PHP Foundation remarked is very unlikely in real-world applications.

Overall, a large number of bugs were fixed and CVEs patched across five releases. Get more info on the PHP news page here.

The November security releases follow a hectic October emergency PHP patch-a-thon, with security teams racing to apply fixes for CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, collectively called PHP2Shell, before attackers could abuse the memory-safety flaws in the open source programming language running on about 70 percent of websites.

While it took miscreants longer to reverse engineer the PHP2Shell fixes than some researchers had anticipated – and the entire internet didn’t burn down in the meantime – the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) did add the two PHP vulns to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on October 26.

Suspected Chinese attackers chained PHP2Shell with a Linux kernel privilege-escalation exploit to root 25 servers, including Palo Alto Networks firewalls linked to US government-affiliated organizations, as early as October 23, according to Dream researchers.

In a recent development, the Israeli AI cybersecurity startup stated the attackers targeted organizations across the US, Japan, Taiwan, and South Korea, and “likely still” have persistent, remote access to compromised organizations’ networks. ®.

Every voice interaction has a latency budget.

According to recent reports, by the time a user hears your application respond, you've already spent precious milliseconds capturing audio, transcribing speech, running an LLM, retrieving context, and generating a response. Text-to-speech (TTS) is the final step — and the one consumers notice most. If speech generation is slow, the whole experience feels slow.

The more of that pipeline you can run and tune yourself, the more of the latency budget you get back.

It has been revealed that voice AI is moving fast. Integrated speech models offer simplicity — one API call, audio in, audio out — but they trade the ability to fine-tune each component for your domain, swap in better models as they ship, enforce data residency, and understand exactly where latency is coming from. For more control, a cascaded architecture — purpose-built ASR, TTS, and LLM components running together — keeps each layer independently tunable and deployable on infrastructure you own.

Sources indicate that NVIDIA Magpie Multilingual TTS is built for that. With open weights, production-ready NVIDIA NIM, and support for 12 languages, you can deploy multilingual speech inside your own infrastructure, optimize latency for your workload, and customize the model for your domain — end to end, in your own environment.

The latest release expands multilingual coverage with Modern Standard Arabic, Korean, and Brazilian Portuguese, while improving quality across many existing languages through updated training data and model improvements.

Whether you're building customer support agents, healthcare assistants, enterprise copilots, translation systems, or conversational AI applications, Magpie provides an open foundation for production voice AI.

Today's voice applications don't serve a single language.

Global customer support, enterprise assistants, healthcare documentation, retail automation, and translation workflows increasingly require natural conversations across multiple languages — all while maintaining low latency.

Magpie TTS Multilingual is a 364M-parameter open-weights model supporting:.

English · Spanish · French · German · Italian · Vietnamese · Mandarin · Hindi · Japanese · Modern Standard Arabic (new) · Korean (new) · Brazilian Portuguese (new).

Each language includes male and female speaker voices through a shared multilingual speaker representation.

This release also improves multilingual flexibility with expanded code-switching support for Hindi and Japanese, enabled through IPA grapheme-to-phoneme processing and custom pronunciation dictionaries — making it easier to accurately pronounce names, technical terminology, and mixed-language content.

Instead of maintaining separate TTS models for different regions, developers can build multilingual applications on a single open foundation.

In conversational AI, text-to-speech is the final stage before users hear a response. That makes Time to First Audio (TTFA) — the delay between speech generation beginning and the first audio reaching the user — one of the most notable latency metrics in a voice pipeline.

Because Magpie TTS can be deployed inside your own environment, the latency you measure is the server-side latency you actually control, with no managed-service round-trip in the number.

Source: NVIDIA TTS NIM Performance documentation (v26.07), average of three trials, on-prem.TTFA = latency to first audio; RTFX = throughput as a multiple of real time.

At 32ms on B200, Magpie's TTFA leaves the rest of the latency budget for ASR and LLM processing — keeping total end-to-end latency within the sub-200ms window natural conversation requires. Across NVIDIA GPUs, Magpie delivers first audio in 32–79ms on a single stream. At 64 concurrent streams, B200 reaches 239ms TTFA while delivering throughput at 320× real time — generating audio more than 300 times faster than it plays back, even under concurrent load.

Because the model runs on your own infrastructure, you can benchmark performance directly, tune it for your deployment, and scale according to your workload. For real-time voice agents, that's the difference between conversations that feel responsive and conversations that feel delayed.

Industry observers note that low latency isn't accidental. Magpie introduces two complementary architectural improvements that reduce inference time while maintaining speech quality.

Frame stacking. The decoder predicts two audio frames during each decoding step rather than one. This cuts the number of decoder iterations in half, shortening generation time and improving throughput.

Local transformer. Frame stacking alone would reduce audio quality by introducing dependencies between simultaneously generated codebook tokens. The local transformer models those dependencies and refines the generated audio, recovering the quality that frame stacking would otherwise sacrifice.

Industry observers note that together, these techniques deliver both faster generation and natural speech synthesis. The architecture is described in Frame-Stacked Local Transformers for Efficient Multi-Codebook Speech Generation (ICASSP 2026).

According to recent reports, this release doesn't only add languages — it also improves synthesis quality across many existing ones. The newly added Arabic (1.62% CER), Korean (2.69%), and Brazilian Portuguese (2.91%) models establish baseline quality for future improvements.

Introducing Amazon ECS Gateway: A fully-managed ingress solution for ECS services

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (877 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When platform teams manage containerized applications at scale on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), configuring ingress networking for each service often becomes a bottleneck.
  • Today, we’re announcing Amazon ECS Gateway, a upcoming account-level resource that simplifies ingress networking for containerized workloads by dynamically provisioning and managing the necessary infrastructure on your behalf, with all resources created directly in your account.
  • ECS Gateway introduces a clear separation of responsibilities between platform teams and application teams.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When platform teams manage containerized applications at scale on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), configuring ingress networking for each service often becomes a bottleneck. For every newly introduced service, teams must provision and connect Application Load Balancers (ALBs), AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificates, AWS WAF web ACLs, and security groups, then keep those resources in sync as services scale, upgrade, or operate. This per-service overhead slows down deployment velocity and increases the risk of configuration drift across an organization.

Today, we’re announcing Amazon ECS Gateway, a upcoming account-level resource that simplifies ingress networking for containerized workloads by dynamically provisioning and managing the necessary infrastructure on your behalf, with all resources created directly in your account.

ECS Gateway introduces a clear separation of responsibilities between platform teams and application teams.

Sources indicate that ECS Gateway offers host-based routing using ALBs and enables up to 25 services to share a single ALB, optimizing infrastructure costs. ECS manages the full lifecycle of the underlying infrastructure, provisioning the first ALB when your first service connects, adding more ALBs as capacity is reached, and removing them when no longer needed. Each service receives a unique DNS hostname, giving your teams a ready-to-use endpoint the moment provisioning completes.

In a recent development, A first look at ECS Gateway In the ECS console, platform team can create a gateway and sets its configuration. The infrastructure role is an IAM role that ECS assumes to provision and manage networking resources such as ALBs, security groups, and certificates in your account. To create a gateway, provide a gateway name and select an infrastructure role. You can optionally associate the gateway with ECS clusters during creation or later.

It has been revealed that choose a load balancing scheme, either public or VPC-internal traffic routing. Under Additional Settings, you can also set up a listener, port, maximum count of load balancers the gateway can scale to, and a web ACL lets you protect your web applications. Some settings, including the name, scheme, VPC, subnets, IP address type, listener protocol and port cannot be changed after gateway creation.

Using AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), call CreateGateway with a name (unique per account), an infrastructure role, and a configuration object. No infrastructure is provisioned until a service connects with a gateway connector.

Once the gateway is created, you can take a look at the detailed configuration, gateway routes, load balancers, and associated clusters.

Now associate the gateway with one or more clusters (many-to-many), to make it available to ECS services on those clusters.

Use AssociateGatewayWithCluster to make the gateway available to services on a cluster:.

To create and manage the ECS Gateway programmatically, including calling APIs and searching documentation, try the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI coding tool. To learn more, visit the Amazon ECS Gateway documentation.

It has been revealed that ECS Gateway:Behind the scenesA gateway can be associated with up to 10,000 clusters, and a single cluster supports up to five gateway associations. This many-to-many relationship gives platform teams the flexibility to share a gateway across environments or assign multiple gateways (for example, public and private) to a single cluster.

It has been revealed that platform teams can control access by choosing which gateways to associate with which clusters. For additional control, use IAM policies to restrict who can deploy services to specific clusters.

Industry observers note that application teams add the gateway connector to each service definition in CreateService or UpdateService. If you have an existing ECS service with its own load balancer, you can adopt ECS Gateway incrementally by calling UpdateService to add a gateway connector. Both ingress paths remain available, allowing you to validate the gateway connection before removing the existing load balancer configuration.

At deployment time, Amazon ECS evaluates the gateways associated with the cluster and connects the service to every compatible gateway. A gateway is compatible when its access type matches the service’s connector filter, it is in the same VPC as the service, and it covers all Availability Zones used by the service’s configured subnets.

For each connection, Amazon ECS assigns the service to an ALB with available capacity and provisions the per-service resources: an ACM certificate, a unique DNS hostname, a listener rule routing traffic for that hostname to the service target group, and a service security group allowing inbound traffic only from the ALB security group. If no existing ALB has capacity, ECS creates a newly introduced one (up to maxAlbCount referring to quota limit). Once provisioning completes, the gateway route becomes ACTIVE, and the service URL is ready to receive traffic.

ECS Gateway handles common operational scenarios automatically:.

Things to Know Here are a few vital details to keep in mind:.

Now available Amazon ECS Gateway is available now in all commercial AWS Regions where ECS is available at no additional charge. You pay only for the underlying infrastructure provisioned in your account when services connect to a gateway, including applicable ALB charges, CloudWatch logs and metrics, ACM certificates, and data transfer charges. To learn more, visit the Amazon ECS Pricing page.

To get started, create your first gateway today in the ECS console, and send feedback to AWS re:Post for ECS or through your usual AWS Support contacts.

  • We built Another Build File Service (ABFS) to address these bottlenecks.
  • Today, we are excited to announce that ABFS is open source on GitHub.The impact of ABFS to Android is:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Android’s source code is big – the Android 17 open source release has 1,084 Git repositories, 1.62 million files, and takes 300 GB for a built workspace. Additionally, in a typical Android source tree with hardware vendor code and first-party applications, the size increases by 2-3x. Traditionally, it took over 30 minutes to fetch Android Open Source Project (AOSP) source code and well over an hour to build on even highly capable developer workstations. As software development evolved over the last 2 years, modern coding harnesses and LLMs have accelerated the development of many projects. These tools are used today for Android operating system development, but the long sync and build times make them less efficient. Both human developers and agents need quick setup, parallel workspaces, and fast build-and-test iteration times.

We built Another Build File Service (ABFS) to address these bottlenecks. ABFS is a full suite of software across a Linux kernel filesystem module, user-space daemons, and server-side infrastructure. ABFS uses content-addressability across the entire stack to lazy-load and cache source code, developer workspaces, intermediate build files, and build results.

Today, we are excited to announce that ABFS is open source on GitHub.The impact of ABFS to Android is:.

ABFS already powers parallel workflows for developers and agents in Android, but it is designed to scale to other massive Git-based projects.

In a recent development, in the Android build system, developers define build rules in Blueprint files (Android.bp), Soong compiles them into Ninja files, and Ninja executes the final build graph (see the Android build overview). Similar to the Make build tool, Ninja is timestamp-based. If a build step’s input file is newer than the existing output file, Ninja rebuilds the output file.

Analyzing the AOSP code for Android 17 shows the sheer disk footprint and file count involved in a single checkout and build.

#69691. Breaking: Thinking of ACE? We Can Do It with Fewer Tokens

📅 11 Aug 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1337 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Thinking of ACE? We Can Do It with Fewer Tokens

📅 11 Aug 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1337 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that ALTK-Evolve and ACE both let an agent learn from its own trajectories.
  • Recent findings suggest that give an LLM agent a realistic multi-step task — split a bill, find a song, reconcile an order across nine simulated apps — and when it fails, it usually isn't for lack of knowledge.
  • Two recent systems do exactly this, on the same kind of agent: ACE (Agentic Context Engineering) and our ALTK-Evolve (introduced here).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that ALTK-Evolve and ACE both let an agent learn from its own trajectories. The difference is what they do with what they learn — and that decides the token bill.

Recent findings suggest that give an LLM agent a realistic multi-step task — split a bill, find a song, reconcile an order across nine simulated apps — and when it fails, it usually isn't for lack of knowledge. It mis-paginates an API, resolves the wrong person, or returns a value when none was asked for. The model knows the APIs; what it hasn't internalized is how to use them reliably. That's learnable from the agent's own history.

Two recent systems do exactly this, on the same kind of agent: ACE (Agentic Context Engineering) and our ALTK-Evolve (introduced here). Both are a form of agentic memory — turning an agent's past trajectories into reusable lessons and feeding them back at inference time, no weight updates, no human labels. They even agree on the hard part. Where they part ways is delivery.

According to recent reports, A note on words, because the two systems name things differently: we'll call the raw thing an agent learns a lesson. ACE organizes its lessons into one comprehensive, evolving playbook; we consolidate ours into individually retrievable guidelines. Same lessons, two containers.

Both systems refuse to compress.

In a recent development, ACE names the failure modes precisely: brevity bias — optimization collapsing toward short, generic instructions — and context collapse — a model asked to rewrite its whole context each step summarizing the detail away. Its answer is to keep a rich, itemized playbook, with a helpful/harmful counter on every bullet, and let the model distill relevance at read time.

We reach the same conclusion from the other direction. Every distinct guideline keeps a support count — how many independent episodes produced it — and we never summarize the store down to a handful of rules. A lesson five different tasks discovered is a different object from one that appeared once, and both are worth keeping.

In a recent development, so on the core question — should you compress an agent's hard-won lessons into a tidy summary? — ACE and ALTK-Evolve give the same answer: no. Count them, don't collapse them. ACE's per-bullet counters and our support counts are two spellings of the same idea.

Two places: how the memory is built, and how it's delivered — and it's the delivery difference that highlights up in the token bill.

Recent findings suggest that consolidation (how the store is built). ACE grows one playbook through a Generator → Reflector → Curator loop, applying incremental delta updates and de-duplicating by embedding. We cluster near-duplicate lessons and merge within a cluster, support-conserving — when several lessons merge, the survivor inherits their combined count, so the store shrinks without losing the record of how much experience backs each guideline. We also extract typed guidelines — strategy, recovery, and optimization — with causal attribution and provenance back to the source trajectory, and at subtask granularity, so a lesson learned on one app can transfer to another.

In a recent development, delivery (what reaches the model at inference). This is the one that drives the numbers. ACE injects the comprehensive playbook on every step, the same way regardless of model or task. We treat delivery as a dial, not a constant: a small fixed core of high-support guidelines, extended per task with a handful selected for the task at hand (cosine or LLM-guided, priority-weighted) — or, when a model has the headroom to use it, the full consolidated set. The same lessons are available to both agents; the difference is that ACE always sends all of them, and we send however many a given model can actually use.

On AppWorld, with the same base ReAct agent, running both systems in-house:.

In a recent development, on the strong model we're better on both metrics at ~40% of ACE's inference cost. On the weak model we edge ACE 56.0 to 54.8 — close enough that we call it a tie on accuracy (a repeat run of ours landed at 54.8, matching ACE almost exactly, which is within this benchmark's run-to-run noise) — at about one-seventh the cost.

A fair word on cost: ACE's own efficiency story is about building its context cheaply. Ours is on a different axis — serving it. Retrieving a few guidelines per task instead of injecting the whole playbook on every step is where the tokens go, and it's the direct consequence of the delivery difference above.

In a recent development, where does the accuracy come from? The by-difficulty breakdown tells two different stories:.

It has been revealed that figure 1. Post-memory Task Goal Completion by difficulty, ours vs. ACE. On DeepSeek-V3.2 (right) we win Easy, Hard, and Overall; ACE only edges Medium. On gpt-oss-120b (left) ACE leads easy and medium, but per-task selection wins the hard tasks — and the aggregate. Each system improves from its own no-memory baseline (see the by-difficulty reference tables under Method notes below).

The two models tell different stories. On gpt-oss-120b, ACE's full playbook has the edge on Easy and Medium — there's enough of the task solved by generic instruction-following that a comprehensive prompt helps more than it distracts. But on Hard tasks, where the model has to pick the right lesson rather than wade through all of them, curated retrieval pulls ahead — and that's the tier that decides the aggregate. On DeepSeek-V3.2 the story flips: the stronger model absorbs ACE's full playbook well enough to edge us on Medium, but we lead Easy, Hard, and Overall — with more capacity to spare, more lessons (delivered our way) keep helping instead of crowding each other out.

We give each model its best configuration — the full consolidated set for the strong model, selective retrieval for the weaker one, because a large context overwhelms a weaker model rather than helping it. (Exactly how much to inject, and how it scales across the capability spectrum, is the focus of our follow-up post.).

According to recent reports, both systems refuse to compress an agent's hard-won experience into a tidy summary — that part, we agree on. The difference is whether delivery is fixed or calibrated: ACE sends the whole playbook every step no matter what; we send however much of the guideline set a given model can actually use. That calibration is what bought the numbers above — same-or-better accuracy at a fraction of ACE's inference cost — and on the weaker model, it was the difference between guidance that helped and guidance that got in the way.

Try the ALTK-Evolve library — which includes the extraction, consolidation, and retrieval pipeline used here — or read the full technical report for the complete method and ablations.

In a recent development, appWorld test_normal, 168 tasks. A ReAct code agent (each step writes Python; the environment returns the output). TGC = Task Goal Completion; SGC = Scenario Goal Completion, which requires every variant of a scenario to pass. Memory is mined from train/dev only; results are single runs (pass@1), as is standard on this benchmark.

Industry observers note that the ACE numbers are our own runs of the ACE agent, evaluated in-house on the same AppWorld splits and the same base models as ALTK-Evolve (DeepSeek-V3.2 and gpt-oss-120b). The ACE paper reports on a different base model (DeepSeek-V3.1), so running it ourselves keeps the comparison controlled for model and harness. Both systems are the same ReAct agent and differ only in the prompt template — which is why the two no-memory baselines differ (72.0 vs 79.8 TGC); we don't rest the comparison on that baseline gap, only on the claims a prompt tweak can't touch: same-or-better accuracy at a fraction of the tokens.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Don’t hoist the Mission Accomplished banner, because company president thinks it also will spur China’s chip biz into action.
  • The USA’s new ban on Chinese companies remotely accessing GPUs will have short-term impact, but ultimately see China accelerate its development of domestic alternatives, according to Martin Lau, the president of Chinese web giant Tencent.
  • Speaking on the manufacturer’s Q3 earnings call, Lau said the upcoming US regulation will have an “unfortunate” impact on Tencent’s business.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Don’t hoist the Mission Accomplished banner, because company president thinks it also will spur China’s chip biz into action.

The USA’s new ban on Chinese companies remotely accessing GPUs will have short-term impact, but ultimately see China accelerate its development of domestic alternatives, according to Martin Lau, the president of Chinese web giant Tencent.

Speaking on the manufacturer’s Q3 earnings call, Lau said the upcoming US regulation will have an “unfortunate” impact on Tencent’s business.

“It does set everyone back. It sets everyone back in China,” Lau said. “So everyone is actually having less advanced compute to work with, no matter when you actually started leasing or building capacities outside of China.”.

He said the ban will impact Tencent’s ability to train models.

In a recent development, “Our training efficiency with Hy4 is actually very high,” he stated. “When we look at the next version, it would take probably longer time for us to come up with the next version in the short run.”.

“But over time, the domestic supply chain would actually come on board.”.

Lau also thinks the bans won’t hamper Tencent’s ability to run inferencing workloads, because made-in-China chips “should be able to cover it.”.

“And over the longer run, we believe all Chinese players would actually have to rely on domestic supply chains and domestic chips, which we see the industry is progressing very fast,” he added. “With the latest restriction, we expect it to actually speed up even further, because all the development effort would actually have to be focused on speeding up the domestic supply chain.”.

Tencent needs GPUs, and lots of them, because the 10 million people of its agentic assistant WorkBuddy are collectively consuming over 100 trillion tokens per day. Lau thinks WorkBuddy is on track to becoming a hit product, partly because many users are outside China.

Lau stated Tencent can serve WorkBuddy customers outside China because the service can operate with different models, and the firm thinks it can find third parties to provide the necessary inferencing services without the latest US bans creating a problem.

But Lau mentioned that GPU rentals and other cloud services, which are also growing strongly, may be impacted.

It has been revealed that “In terms of cloud, if it is non-GPU related, we can actually build capacities ourselves outside of China,” he said. “I think there is still a lot of such opportunities because our cloud service is actually very cost competitive. When it comes to GPU, then unfortunately, we cannot actually offer high-end GPU anymore. We may be able to work with some partners in different places.”.

Recent findings suggest that tencent doesn’t break out revenue for its cloud services, but said they rose by 35 percent year-on-year, well ahead of the firm’s overall eight percent growth. Marketing services also grew strongly, by 19 percent, thanks in part to newly introduced AI-powered systems that improve ad targeting.

The company’s WeChat and Weixin messaging platforms continued to grow, adding 35 million accounts to exiting the quarter with 1.44 billion monthly active people.

One Tencent biz that went backwards was its international gaming unit, which saw revenue fall nine percent.

Chief strategy officer James Mitchell remarked that slowdown wasn’t caused by the release of Grand Theft Auto VI. “I think that in fairness, the slowdown for us predated the run-up to GTA VI,” he said, before predicting that Tencent’s existing and future “evergreen games” should help to turn things around.

AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is now generally available

📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1244 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today, we’re announcing the general availability of AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities.
  • According to recent reports, using frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models, threat actors can turn a vulnerability disclosure into working exploit code in minutes, and the same tools that speed up development also increase the volume of findings your teams must process.
  • Industry observers note that continuum builds a context graph from two primary sources: your code repositories and your AWS environment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, we’re announcing the general availability of AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities. AWS Continuum is a security service that finds and validates code vulnerabilities, then delivers fixes as patches you can automate or as pull requests in your repositories. AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities confirms which findings are exploitable in your environment, ranks the resulting issues by business impact, and proposes a fix for each one. Every remediation starts in a mode where Continuum proposes the fix and a person approves it before it ships. In the future, you will be able to decide which actions Continuum can take on its own, within the guardrails you define.

According to recent reports, using frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models, threat actors can turn a vulnerability disclosure into working exploit code in minutes, and the same tools that speed up development also increase the volume of findings your teams must process. If your organization runs a large application estate, your scanners likely produce thousands of findings a day, and many of them need no action. A finding can be unreachable, unexploitable, or already mitigated by a runtime control. Generic severity scores don’t tell you which resources a threat actor can actually reach, so a critical score on a dev-only utility looks the same as a medium score on a service one step away from a payments database. Previously, confirming whether a finding was exploitable took hours of manual investigation, and shipping a fix with confidence took days of coordination across security, infrastructure, and application teams, because the blast radius of a change is hard to assess without business context. To close that gap, Continuum proves which findings are exploitable and bounds the risk of each fix it proposes.

Industry observers note that continuum builds a context graph from two primary sources: your code repositories and your AWS environment. For AWS, you set up a collector in the account and Region where your code runs. The collector gathers resource details such as AWS Config resources and network configuration so Continuum can judge whether a vulnerability is reachable over the network and what a threat actor could reach from it. From this graph, Continuum learns which systems are business-critical, who owns them, how services depend on one another, and which data each one touches. It uses that picture to identify your highest-value systems, such as customer data stores, payment pipelines, and authentication services, and then ranks each resulting issue by how close its attack path runs to those systems.

Continuum analyzes each finding against your code and its environment context and assigns an evidence level, such as a verdict proven by static analysis of the vulnerable code path. For findings it can reproduce, Continuum runs the exploit in an isolated sandbox and attaches proof-of-concept code with the reproduction steps. It produces the attack path, the supporting source analysis, and a blast radius assessment instead of a risk score alone. It also evaluates whether your existing defenses would detect and stop the validated path.

According to recent reports, for each confirmed matter, Continuum generates a fix (a code patch, a dependency upgrade, or a configuration change) and opens it as a pull request in your connected repository, ready to review. Every fix requires human approval: you review and merge the pull request, so the final decision stays with your team. In the future, you will be able to build confidence in specific remediation classes and let Continuum apply those fixes automatically once its confidence gates pass, such as test coverage, scope bounds, and historical success rate.

According to recent reports, AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities in actionTo show how this works, I open AWS Continuum in the console and go to Code vulnerabilities. Before I can review issues, I set up an environment. I connect a code source, either a GitHub integration or an Amazon S3 bucket, and then create an environment that scans it on a schedule I choose. An Amazon S3 source has a couple of prerequisites: the bucket sits in the same account and AWS Region where I turn on AWS Continuum, and I grant access through an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role that AWS Continuum assumes. I can optionally add AWS infrastructure context by setting up an AWS Continuum collector in the account and Region where my code runs and authorizing my environment to use it. For the full requirements and steps, see the AWS Continuum User Guide.

The Overview page brings these pieces together in one place, showing my Code integrations, the Environments built on them, and the status of any AWS collector that supplies AWS resource context.

I open one of my environments. The Issues tab lists validated, prioritized issues rather than raw scanner output, each with a severity, a status, and the time it was created. I choose one of the issues.

The Overview rates it High severity, with the status Completed and the remediation already Delivered to GitHub. The Risk assessment explains why. Continuum rates its Exploitability as Exploitable, with an evidence level of Static proven and a validation run status of Completed. Likelihood is High, since the service is reachable from an attacker, requires no authentication, and needs no user interaction. Impact is Moderate, which means an attacker gains the ability to modify business data, with a blast radius reaching other users in the same tenant. A Proof section includes the source analysis behind the verdict.

Sources indicate that the Remediation section demonstrates a fix already delivered as a pull request in GitHub, changing four files, with 50 lines added and 24 removed across the cart service. Continuum opens the fix as a pull request titled Continuum fix, and I choose View pull request to open it in GitHub. The console is explicit that a generated patch does not mean the glitch is fixed. I still review and merge it, which keeps the final decision with my team. A Contributing findings section lists the specific scanner finding this issue was built from.

The pull request description carries the same risk assessment, remediation summary, and proof from the console, so whoever reviews it in GitHub sees the evidence without leaving their workflow.

The Findings tab lists the raw scanner findings across the environment, the evidence that concerns are built from.

According to recent reports, the Scans tab indicates the history of each scan with its status, origin, and request and completion times, and I use Configure scan frequency to change the cadence or Queue scan to run one on demand. The Configuration tab is where I manage the environment: the code and context sources it reads from, its code integrations, environment settings such as whether Continuum creates remediation patches, and the AWS collectors it uses for AWS context.

In a recent development, in a single workflow, I work through the validated concerns in priority order with each scan, reviewing the evidence and scope behind each one before I approve and merge the fixes I trust. Every fix waits for my approval, so the backlog keeps shrinking while my team keeps control of what ships.

Now available AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is available today in US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon) Regions. For pricing, visit the pricing page.

To learn more, visit the AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities product page and the User Guide. Give it a try in the AWS Continuum console today, and send us feedback through your usual AWS Support contacts.
